facts.text: It is colloquially known as the moth owl or fairy owl, and the Warlpiri people call it Jarlajirrpi.
facts.quote: It is colloquially known as the moth owl or fairy owl and Jarlajirrpi by the Warlpiri people.

facts.text: The Australian owlet-nightjar has large dark eyes that do not reflect light, unlike many other nocturnal birds.
facts.quote: It has large dark eyes that are non-reflective when a light is shone upon them; unlike many other nocturnal birds.

facts.text: When disturbed, some owlet-nightjars puff up, sway side to side, open their mouths wide to show a pink gape and hiss.
facts.quote: There are a few anecdotal reports of Australian owlet-nightjars flattening themselves or puffing up to seem larger, swaying side to side, opening their mouths wide to show their pink gape and hissing.

facts.text: Pairs are thought to mate for life, breeding between August and December, with the female incubating three or four eggs for just under a month.
facts.quote: Australian owlet-nightjar pairs are thought to mate for life, and pairs breed between August and December. Three or four eggs are laid and incubated by the female for just under a month.

facts.text: Nest holes are lined with eucalyptus leaves by both parents, thought to act as a beneficial insecticide.
facts.quote: which are provisioned with leaves by both of the pair. It is thought that the frequent addition of eucalyptus leaves is because they act as a beneficial insecticide.

facts.text: In winter it often enters torpor daily, usually around dawn for 3-4 hours, to conserve energy.
facts.quote: They usually enter torpor once a day around dawn for 3–4 hours, if they enter torpor twice in a day it is always a morning bout followed by a bout in the afternoon or night.

facts.text: It is 21–25 cm long, with grey upperparts, a white barred front and dark and pale patterning on the head.
facts.quote: It is 21–25 cm long, making it a small to medium-sized owlet-nightjar with grey upperparts and a white, barred front and a distinct dark and pale patterning on the head.

facts.text: It is frequently heard but not often seen, with calls described as churr, cry, yuk, cho-ok, hiss and screech.
facts.quote: Adult Australian owlet-nightjars appear to have a few main calls described as: "churr, cry, yuk, cho-ok, hiss, screech and other short harsh rattling notes".

facts.text: On average it moves between roost sites over about 300 m every nine days, and may use two to six different cavities over six months.
facts.quote: On average they move between roost sites over a distance of about 300 m every nine days and in one study used between two and six different cavities over a six month period.

facts.text: It prefers hunting on moonlit nights, but on full moon nights hunts only enough to meet its energy requirements.
facts.quote: this is likely why their hunting behaviour is reduced on nights with full moons, when they only hunt enough to meet their energy requirements.
